/itineraryStops/1/smartNotes/tip.source_en: OPT FOR THE MONORAIL (additional ~3,000 KRW vs walking) if you are: 65+ years old, taller than 1.95 m, prone to claustrophobia, have heart/lung/back issues, or have weak knees. The walking-ramp return at 11° is the day's hardest physical demand. Wear sturdy closed-toe shoes — floor uneven and damp.

/itineraryStops/1/smartNotes/facilities.source_en: DMZ Video Room (10-min orientation film), DMZ Exhibition Hall on Korean War + DMZ ecosystem, souvenir shops at surface. Fresh-water tap inside the tunnel for visitors with claustrophobia or fatigue.

/itineraryStops/1/whyOnRoute.source_en: The 3rd Tunnel is the day's most physically and emotionally substantial DMZ stop. No other site on the Korean peninsula gives visitors a literal in-the-tunnel experience of inter-Korean conflict — the spy-hole at the end of the tunnel, only 170 m from the actual border with North Korea, makes the divided peninsula tangible in a way no museum can replicate. For private-charter guests this is also the day's most logistically rigid stop — monorail tickets are capped at 150/day, photography and electronics are confiscated before descent, and the Korea Tourism Organization's reservation system requires a passport-or-ARC ID check at the Civilian Control Line just beyond Unification Bridge. Mondays, Seollal, and Chuseok are full closure days — your driver-guide pre-validates the day's reservation slot the morning of departure to avoid a wasted 70-minute drive from Seoul on a closure day.

/itineraryStops/1/description.source_en:
Discovered October 17, 1978 — the third of four North Korean infiltration tunnels found under the DMZ, and the closest to Seoul at just 52 km. South Korean / U.S. Army Far East District drilling teams located it 15 meters ahead of where the joint team had been excavating after detecting an underground explosion (a faulty dynamite charge) on June 10 that year, four months before the formal discovery. 

The tunnel runs 1,635 meters in total length, 1.95 m at maximum height and 2.1 m wide, through bedrock at approximately 73 m below ground — designed to enable around 30,000 troops per hour with light weaponry to surge into Seoul. 

When discovered, North Korea claimed the South had dug it; the directional evidence of the dynamite charges (oriented southward) plus later coal-painting on the walls (in a clumsy attempt to claim the tunnel was a coal mine, despite the bedrock geology containing no coal) confirmed the North's responsibility. 

Visitors descend either via a 350-meter steeply graded (~11°) walking ramp or via a slow rubber-tyred monorail to reach the tunnel level, then walk a further 358 m horizontally to the first of three concrete blockades the South Korean military installed at the Military Demarcation Line — a spy-hole through the blockade allows a peek northward, only 170 m from the actual border. 

Photography is strictly forbidden inside the tunnel; cameras and phones are checked into lockers before descent. The South Koreans located the tunnel via a North Korean defector tip combined with underground-explosion sensor detection in June 1978. 

After **four months of intercept-tunnel drilling**, the joint US Army Far East District / ROK Army team broke through to the tunnel on October 17, 1978. 

Visitor entry is via the dedicated DMZ Peace Tour shuttle from Imjingak only — independent vehicle access is prohibited.
